excerpts.text: A novel heterozygous mutation of BCL11B gene causes neurodevelopmental disorder and middle type hypospadias in a Chinese boy with 5 years follow-up

As a crucial transcription factor, BCL11 transcription factor B gene (BCL11B) is expressed in the cell nucleus, and also widely expressed in the nervous and immune systems. Function of BCL11B varied, mutation of BCL11B gene may involve diverse diseases, such as immunodeficiency 49 (IMD49) and intellectual developmental disorder with speech delay, dysmorphic facies, and T-cell abnormalities (IDDSFTA). Here we reported a Chinese boy with significant neurodevelopmental delay, whose genetic exam revealed the BCL11B gene mutation. During the 5-year follow-up, no serious immune system defects and infections were found, but some autism spectrum disorders gradually emerged, and the patient was finally diagnosed with IDDSFTA caused by BCL11B mutation. This study is the first to report the phenotypic association between BCL11B gene mutation and moderate hypospadias. Although a previous study has documented the co-occurrence of this gene mutation with hypospadias, the hypospadias in that case was of the mild form. The moderate phenotype presented in this case significantly expands the clinical spectrum of BCL11B-associated disorders.
Introduction

BCL11 transcription factor B gene (BCL11B), as a Cys2-his2 zinc finger protein transcription factor, located in 14q32.2, widely expressed not only mainly in hematologic and lymphatic systems, but also in the nervous system. BCL11B precisely participated in regulated organs' function and play crucial roles in the different tissues physiological functions, to allow the highly specialized plasticity of body. Lessel et al. hold the view that reports apparently described that patients carrying pathogenic mutation BCL11B display intellectual disabilities and neurological disorders, but remain not fully understood for the detailed molecular mechanisms. In animal experiment, conditional deletion of BCL11B caused loss of excitatory synapses and abnormal synaptic transmission . Emerging studies demonstrated BCL11B execute key roles are associated with two dysplasia syndromes including the immunodeficiency 49 (IMD49) and intellectual developmental disorder with speech delay, dysmorphic facies, and T-cell abnormalities (IDDSFTA). These above-mentioned disorders have some overlapping clinical features, including distinctive facial features, psychomotor developmental delay, language impairment, and immune dysfunction. However, IDDSFTA also accompanied by autism spectrum disorders (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and other abnormalities in developmental behavior. Focusing on the clinical manifestation, the hazard of IDDSFTA is relatively milder than that of IMD49.

Herein, we report a proband presenting with distinctive facial features, microcephaly (small head circumference), abnormal enamel development, mild immune function abnormalities, developmental delay complicated with autism, and moderate hypospadias:this latter phenotype further expands the clinical phenotypic spectrum of the disorder. The proband was ultimately diagnosed with a novel heterozygous mutation in the BCL11B gene, which provides additional support for the association between this mutation and the syndrome.
Case Description

A boy aged 18 months, who was admitted to our hospital due to 12 months of developmental delay. The parents were non-consanguineous with no family history of genetic disorders. During the fetal period, the patient experienced intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). For the reason of severe preeclampsia of his mother's complication, at 33+6 weeks of gestation, he was born by the cesarean section. The proband Apgar scores were 7, 8 and 9 points at 1, 5, and 10 min respectively after time of birth, and birth weight was 1050 g (below the 3rd percentile for infants of the same sex and gestational age: 1400 g) and the body length was 36 cm (below the 3rd percentile for infants of the same sex and gestational age: 38.7cm).

Facial features of the patient. (A) Brachycephaly; (B) Thin eyebrows, wide-set eyes, low-set ears, long philtrum; (C) Dental anomalies (These images were captured in November 2021, when the patient was 5 years old.)
Cranial MRI of the patient (T1-weighted). (A) Slightly dilated lateral ventricles bilaterally; (B) Slightly widened extracerebral space in the frontal-parietal lobes bilaterally
Lymphocyte subset analysis of the patient

Physical examination of this patient revealed a small head circumference and brachycephaly, special facial features including thin eyebrows, wide-set eyes, low-set ears, and a long philtrum (Fig. 1). Besides the above-mentioned appearance, this boy also had enamel dysplasia and a surgical scar on the penis. The weight was 8.7kg (the 3rd percentile value for individuals of the same sex and age is 9.19kg), height was 76 cm (the 3rd percentile value for individuals of the same sex and age is 76.9cm) and head circumference was 45.7cm (the 5th percentile value for individuals of the same sex and age is 45.7cm) of the patient at 18 months old. The brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed at 4-year-old of the patient, result indicated slight dilation of the lateral ventricles on both sides and slightly widened extracerebral space in the bilateral frontal and parietal lobes (Fig. 2). Blood laboratory examinations were also finished in our case, first, we completed blood routine examination of this patient at 18-month-old, result showed that nearly all the results were normal, including cell counts of white blood cell, red blood cell, blood platelet, lymphocyte, hemoglobin, neutrophil, eosinophils. Besides, other laboratory examinations were also unremarkable, including blood calcium, vitamin D, bone metabolism markers, and thyroid function had no significant abnormal. Immunological examination revealed IgA, IgG, and IgM were all normal. Cellular immunity indicated that the absolute counts of B cells and T cells were normal, but existed a slight reduction in the CD3 + T cell/B cell ratio, and normal NK cell count (Table 1). Furthermore, Developmental milestones were described as follows: the patient could stand with support but could not walk, could not call mom or dad consciously, avoided eye contact with other people, demonstrated a lack of response to name calling, exhibited stereotyped behaviors such as banging blocks, and had difficulties in the social interaction even at 18 months old. The results of the Gesell Developmental Diagnosis Scale indicated that the patient had global developmental delay. Developmental quotients (DQs) in the domains of adaptability, gross motor, fine motor, language, and personal-social skills were 32.91, 61.46, 52.92, 54.63, and 53.21, respectively. These findings revealed a severe deficit in adaptability, moderate deficits in fine motor skills, language, and personal-social skills, and a mild delay in gross motor development.

Pedigree of the family and Sanger sequencing analysis. (A) The pedigree of the patient's family; (B) A heterozygous mutation c.1176_1179dup (p.Pro394Glufs*124) in the BCL11B gene is observed in the patient, but no mutation is observed at this locus in his parents

Chromosomal analysis showed 46,XY. Peripheral blood samples were obtained from the proband and both biological parents, with biological parenthood confirmed through clinical and pedigree information. Genomic DNA was extracted using the Hieff NGS OnePot Pro DNA Library Prep Kit (Yeasen Biotechnology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.), followed by trio-based whole-exome sequencing (Trio-WES). Analysis identified a heterozygous frameshift variant in the BCL11B gene, corresponding to the canonical transcript NM_138576.4. This variant, located within exon 4, involves a 4-nucleotide duplication (c.1176_1179dup) that leads to a premature termination codon at position 124 of the altered reading frame (p.Pro394Glufs*124). (Fig. 3). According to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines for the classification of genetic variants, this variant is pathogenic (PVS1 + PS2 + PM2_Supporting). Subsequent Sanger sequencing validated the variant in the proband and confirmed its absence in both parental samples, thereby establishing its de novo status.

Growth curve of the patient (The curve was plotted according to the standardized growth curves for Chinese children established by the Growth and Development Research Laboratory of the Capital Institute of Pediatrics.). (A) Percentile growth curves for weight and length from 0 to 3 years of age; (B) Percentile growth curve for head circumference from 0 to 3 years of age; (C) Percentile growth curves for weight and height from 2 to 5 years of age; (D) Standard deviation growth curves for weight and height from 2 to 5 years of age

The patient continued to undergo rehabilitation training and nutritional management. At 3-year-old, he was able to perform a high jump, had the ability to express simple sentences but no more than 10 words, communicate with some familiar age children, consciously call people title, but still avoided eye contact with other person. At the age of five, he was able to ascend stairs by alternating steps on his own, jump off the ground with both feet but unable to stand on one foot unsupported. He could stack up to three blocks but did not have the ability to knock them together. In terms of language, the patient could speak short phrases of including five to six words, but yet his execution of simple commands was subpar. Regarding personal and social skills, he could remove his shoes and socks by himself and could dress and undress with assistance for simple garments. However, he exhibited no obvious imitative behavior in daily life and did not engage in cooperative play with peers. Reassessment using the Griffiths Mental Development Scales (GMDS) demonstrated persistent global developmental delay, with marked deficits specifically in the Personal-Social, Hearing and Speech, Eye-Hand Coordination, Visual-Performance, and Practical Reasoning domains. During standardized testing, the patient exhibited poor response to name calling and displayed repetitive stereotypic behaviors, which necessitated a comprehensive structured interview with the caregiver utilizing the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) protocol. The ADI-R demonstrated scores exceeding diagnostic thresholds across core domains: social domain (16 points, above the cutoff score of 10), communication and language domain (16 points, above the cutoff score of 8), and restricted/repetitive behaviors domain (5 points, above the cutoff score of 3). Combined with the presence of developmental abnormalities emerging before 36 months of age, these findings are consistent with ASD, diagnosed by a developmental pediatrician according to DSM-5 criteria. Currently, his height, weight, and head circumference were still below those of his peers (Fig. 4).
Discussion

BCL11B is a zinc finger protein transcription factor of the Kruppel family, encoding a C2H2 zinc finger protein. Emerging evidence demonstrated that BCL11B plays crucial roles in transcriptional activation or inhibition by regulating expression of downstream genes in a time and region specific manner, furthermore, plays a regulatory or even decisive role in various physiological processes such as T lymphocytes, as well as cell survival. BCL11B is widely expressed in various cell types and is closely related to central nervous system development, including axon formation and neuronal differentiation. Furthermore, studies have established that mutant BCL11B is associated with neurodevelopmental disorders and T cell deficiency. However, the total number of reported patients is limited. Moreover, the full spectrum of clinical phenotypes and the detailed distinctions among them remain incompletely understood. Although IUGR may have contributed to the growth and developmental outcomes, the syndromic facial, dental, and behavioral features, together with the de novo loss-of-function (LoF) variant, are more consistent with and strongly support a diagnosis of a BCL11B-related disorder. Compared to previously documented cases, our report introduces a new clinical manifestation:moderate hypospadias:caused by a novel BCL11B mutation, which may expand the phenotypic spectrum of BCL11B-related disorder. In current studies, the phenotypic spectrum and diagnostic boundaries of IMD49 and IDDSFTA show partial overlap, including craniofacial developmental abnormalities, hypotonia, intellectual disability, and language disorders. However, the two reported cases of IMD49 both presented with dermatitis in the neonatal period (one case of erythematous psoriasis-like dermatitis, one case of congenital erosive dermatitis), cardiovascular malformations (one case of mild pulmonary stenosis, one case of mild aortic dilation), and severe combined immunodeficiency (decreased leukocyte count with varying degrees of reduction in T cell receptor excision circles, with one case not detecting T cell receptor excision circles).

Compared with other reported patients, in our case, the patient presented with craniofacial developmental abnormalities (thin eyebrows, wide-set eyes, long philtrum), dental caries and malocclusion, hypospadias, comprehensive developmental delay (including gross motor, fine motor, language, and personal-social), and signs of autism. The patient's immunological examination only showed an abnormal B/T cell ratio, with normal absolute values of B and T cells, and other innate immune cells. During the follow-up time, there was no history of recurrent infection or related congenital immunodeficiency, and we also made blood routine examination of that patient, results of the cells count nearly all normal. Genotype-phenotype correlation has not been fully understood, genotypes may produce complex clinical-behavioral phenotypes. Through come from the same given genotype, phenotype was not always expressed in the same manner. We guess that this disease is dominantly inherited, but the penetrance may affect the clinical manifestations of children to varying degrees.

Our patient's overall phenotypic presentation, combined with Trio-WES results demonstrating the LoF frameshift variant, supports the diagnosis of IDDSFTA. Furthermore, we compared the clinical phenotypes of patients with BCL11B mutations and our patient phenotypes (Table 2) We noticed that, unlike previous clinical phenotypes, this case had a significant hypospadias (middle type), which had been treated with early surgery. Notably, no other pathogenic variants potentially associated with middle-type hypospadias were identified through Trio-WES in this analysis. A comparison of hypospadias was that Alfei et al. previously reported a patient with a BCL11B gene mutation combined with hypospadias, but the degree of hypospadias in that patient was mild, only presented as glanular hypospadias (anterior type). Male urethra is a tubular urethra formed from the proximal to distal urethral plate, and the final step in penile development is the circular development of the foreskin. In hypospadias, the penile fascia and skin fail to develop normally on the ventral side of the penis between 8-12 weeks of gestation, and incomplete fusion of the urethral groove results in ectopic urethral opening. As a top-level regulator of skin morphogenesis, BCL11B is highly expressed in the skin during development and plays a key role in the proliferation and late differentiation of keratinocytes. Mutation of BCL11B expression may cause maturation disorders of urothelial cells, leading to rupture of the urothelium and the formation of hypospadias. It is currently believed that anterior hypospadias is often caused by multiple gene mutations or various other factors, while posterior hypospadias is more likely to be a monogenic mutation disease. The discovery of BCL11B mutation in a patient with middle hypospadias raises the question of whether BCL11B can be consider a candidate gene for severe clinical phenotypes of hypospadias. From the perspective of clinical practice, this finding indicates that for patients carrying BCL11B gene mutations, a more comprehensive and detailed assessment of the genitourinary system should be conducted even if no obvious abnormalities are observed in the early stage.

Following the initial genetic data analysis of this case, the patient gradually presented new clinical phenotypes. Consequently, a re-analysis of the sequencing data was initiated; although the BCL11B variant was initially interpreted as likely pathogenic, it was subsequently upgraded based on the evolving clinical evidence, and we herein report its final classification as pathogenic. Combined with literature reports, the patient's diagnosis of IDDSFTA was finally confirmed after one year. The transcription factor BCL11B plays pivotal roles in the development of multiple physiological systems, including immune, neural, craniofacial, and cutaneous systems. It shows a complex biologic of function in the diseases. Cismasiu et al. reported that reduced BCL11B expression diminishes IL-2 promoter activity in activated CD4 + T cells. IL-2 is essential for T-cell proliferation and helps maintain T cell homeostasis during the late stage of the antigen-specific T cell response. Studies had also demonstrated that BCL11B mediates neuronal differentiation. Further research showed the implication of BCL11B involved in regulating neurogenesis in spatial working memory in animal model. Additionally, BCL11B is expressed in osteogenic mesenchyme of the developing craniofacial complex, particularly during specific embryonic developmental windows. Kyrylkova K et al. demonstrated through conditional knockout (Bcl11bncc-/-) and global knockout (Bcl11b-/-) mouse models that BCL11B deficiency results in craniofacial skeletal abnormalities. In 2018, Lessel et al. reported 13 patients with BCL11B heterozygous mutations, all of whom had facial developmental malformations, intellectual disabilities, and language disorders. Twelve patients had delayed motor development, five had dental abnormalities, four exhibited autism traits, and three suffered from refractive errors. Among them, eight patients underwent lymphocyte immunotyping, revealed that all patients had normal NK cell proportions, two had slightly increased B lymphocyte proportions, and the percentage of T lymphocytes was relatively reduced. Further T lymphocyte immunotyping indicated that all patients had increased proportions of gammaT cells and varying degrees of reduction in CD4 + recent thymic emigrants (RTE), suggesting impaired T cell development. However, in 2020, Yan et al. reported a case of a Chinese child with IDDSFTA, whose gammadeltaT cell and CD4 + RTE percentages were within the reference range. And another compelling aspect of the researchers' view, reported by Roa-Bautista A et al. showed an even increased absolute count of T lymphocytes, similar to the data described by Yan et al.. In the Yang et al. article they hold the view that absence of functional BCL11B may resulted in the damage of brain white matter, which in turn resulted in the neurodevelopmental disorder and the heterozygous frameshift mutation in the BCL11B. In a recent study, Seigfried et al. highlighted that BCL11B mediates neuronal differentiation and regulates synaptic vesicle organization. Loss of BCL11B induces axonal and synaptic alterations, resulting in impaired signal transduction, which represents a key determinant of neurodevelopmental disorders. In our case, the patient also has the cognitive function impairment and mutation in the BCL11B. Maintaining the balance between gain- and loss-of-function of BCL11B is important. Furthermore, the above-mentioned studies prompted additional evaluation for BCL11B in immune cells and neurodevelopmental disorder. However, patients did not show severe immune deficiencies, and there were no significant abnormalities in cellular immunity and humoral immunity, requiring long-term follow-up to further clarify whether there is immune function defects exist. In our case, mild immunophenotypic deviations were noted (e.g., lower CD4/CD8 and CD3 + T cell/B cell) without recurrent infections to date; therefore, longitudinal follow-up is warranted.

It is crucial to delineate the molecular mechanisms underlying the observed heterogeneous phenotypes, as this distinction often dictates the severity of the syndrome. IDDSFTA is generally associated with LoF variants, resulting in BCL11B haploinsufficiency. This mechanism is consistent with our patient's identified heterozygous frameshift mutation (c.1176_1179dup, p.Pro394Glufs*124), which is predicted to be a functional null allele. Such LoF mutations typically lead to a milder neurodevelopmental phenotype with variable T cell abnormalities, generally without the severe multisystem anomalies characteristic of IMD49. In contrast, IMD49 is linked to specific missense mutations (such as p.N441K and p.N807K) which operate via a dominant negative or gain-of-function (GoF) mechanism. Functional studies of the IMD49-associated p.N441K mutation demonstrated that the mutant protein forms nonfunctional heterodimers with wild type BCL11B, impairing binding to known canonical sites while simultaneously promoting abnormal binding to novel genomic regions. This GoF mechanism is believed to be responsible for the more severe IMD49 clinical outcome, which includes SCID, profound developmental delay, and major multisystem anomalies (such as callosal agenesis and severe dermatitis). Our case supports that the LoF mechanism of BCL11B results in IDDSFTA, although its broad pleiotropic role in immune, neural, craniofacial, and cutaneous systems suggests that mutational effects may be modulated by other genetic modifiers or environmental factors, thereby contributing to broader clinical heterogeneity, such as the observed moderate hypospadias. Future research is essential to collect more cases, further enrich the clinical phenotypes, and deeply explore the specific molecular mechanisms underlying these phenotypes of varying severity.
Conclusions

This study is the first to report the phenotypic association between BCL11B gene mutation and moderate hypospadias. This finding not only provides stronger support for the assertion that "BCL11B gene mutation is a pathogenic cause of specific syndromes" but also suggests that this gene may be involved in the development of the urogenital system. However, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Future studies are needed to collect more cases to further enrich the clinical phenotypes and genetic variation spectrum of this syndrome, and to deeply explore the specific molecular mechanisms underlying its phenotypes of varying severity. Different from other cases with IDDSFTA, this patient is one of the relatively longer follow-up cases, which demonstrated the long-term survival outcomes and quality of life.
